blocks.text: A 19-year-old footballer plants his foot, twists, and hears a pop. Within an hour the knee is swollen with blood and it gives way when he tries to turn. The anatomy of four strong bands in the knee, and of two C-shaped cartilages, explains the injury and the examination that identifies it.

blocks.markdown: The **knee** is the largest synovial joint, a modified hinge between the femur and tibia with a separate articulation between the patella and the femur. Because its bony surfaces fit poorly, stability depends almost entirely on **ligaments**, **menisci** and the surrounding muscles. The **leg** contains the tibia and fibula, which connect to the **ankle** (talocrural joint) and the **foot**, whose bones form arches that support weight.

blocks.title: Menisci
blocks.text: Two C-shaped wedges of fibrocartilage on the tibial plateau, medial and lateral. They deepen the articular surface, absorb shock and spread load across the joint. The medial meniscus is larger and is firmly attached to the tibial (medial) collateral ligament, which makes it less mobile and more likely to be torn; the lateral meniscus is smaller, nearly circular and more mobile, and it is not attached to the fibular collateral ligament.

rows: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)
Anterior intercondylar area of the tibia to the medial surface of the lateral femoral condyle
Prevents the tibia sliding forwards on the femur; resists hyperextension and rotation
Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL)
Posterior intercondylar area of the tibia to the lateral surface of the medial femoral condyle
Prevents the tibia sliding backwards on the femur; important when the knee is flexed
Tibial (medial) collateral ligament
Medial femoral epicondyle to the medial surface of the tibia; attached to the medial meniscus
Resists valgus (outward angulation) force
Fibular (lateral) collateral ligament
Lateral femoral epicondyle to the head of the fibula; separate from the lateral meniscus
Resists varus (inward angulation) force
blocks.caption: The main ligaments stabilising the knee.

blocks.markdown: The cruciate ligaments lie inside the capsule and cross each other like an X, hence the name. They are named by their tibial attachment: the anterior one attaches to the anterior part of the tibia, the posterior one to the posterior part. The quadriceps tendon, patella and patellar ligament form an extensor mechanism in front, and the muscles around the joint, especially quadriceps, contribute to dynamic stability.

blocks.title: ACL injury and its clinical test
blocks.text: The ACL is usually torn in non-contact injuries involving sudden deceleration, hyperextension or a pivoting twist on a planted foot, for example in football, netball or skiing. Patients often hear a pop and develop rapid swelling from bleeding into the joint (haemarthrosis) within hours; the knee gives way when turning. The anterior drawer test (with the knee flexed to about 90 degrees, the examiner pulls the tibia forwards) and the more sensitive Lachman test (with the knee in about 20 to 30 degrees of flexion) show excess forward movement of the tibia on the femur when the ACL is torn.

blocks.title: Which ligament is torn?
blocks.prompt: In an examination the tibia of a patient moves further forward than normal on the femur when pulled with the knee in 30 degrees of flexion, and there is no abnormal opening of the joint with sideways stress. Which ligament is torn?

steps.text: Forward displacement of the tibia on the femur is restrained by the ACL.
A posterior drawer (backward displacement) would indicate the PCL, so it is not implicated.
Normal sideways stress testing makes a collateral ligament tear unlikely.

blocks.answer: The anterior cruciate ligament (positive Lachman test).

blocks.markdown: **The unhappy triad.** A sideways blow to the outside of the knee when the foot is fixed (a valgus force with rotation) can tear the **tibial collateral ligament**, the attached **medial meniscus** and the **anterior cruciate ligament** together. This is the classic 'unhappy triad' (O'Donoghue triad).

**Leg and ankle.** The leg skeleton is the weight-bearing **tibia** medially and the slender **fibula** laterally, joined by the interosseous membrane. Distally the tibia (medial malleolus) and fibula (lateral malleolus) form a mortise that grips the **talus** at the **ankle joint**. Medially the strong **deltoid ligament** resists eversion; laterally the **anterior talofibular ligament** is the weakest and the one most often sprained in inversion injuries.

**Arches of the foot.** The foot has three arches, which distribute weight between the heel (calcaneus) and the heads of the metatarsals (the ball of the foot) and give the foot elasticity. The **medial longitudinal arch** is high and springy: it is formed by the calcaneus, talus, navicular, three cuneiforms and the medial three metatarsals. The **lateral longitudinal arch** is low and rigid: calcaneus, cuboid and the lateral two metatarsals. The **transverse arch** runs across the midfoot at the level of the cuneiforms and cuboid.

rows: Medial longitudinal
Calcaneus, talus, navicular, three cuneiforms, medial three metatarsals
Plantar calcaneonavicular (spring) ligament, plantar aponeurosis, tibialis posterior, flexor hallucis longus and tibialis anterior tendons
Lateral longitudinal
Calcaneus, cuboid, lateral two metatarsals
Long and short plantar ligaments, fibularis longus and brevis tendons
Transverse
Cuboid, cuneiforms and bases of metatarsals
Fibularis longus tendon, tibialis posterior, adductor hallucis (transverse head), deep transverse metatarsal ligaments
blocks.caption: Arches of the foot and the structures maintaining them (bones, ligaments and tendons).

blocks.title: Flat foot after tendon injury
blocks.prompt: A patient with chronic failure of the tibialis posterior tendon develops a flat foot. Explain the mechanism.

steps.text: Tibialis posterior passes behind the medial malleolus and inserts on the navicular and neighbouring tarsal bones, supporting the medial longitudinal arch.
If the tendon fails, the support to the navicular and spring ligament is lost, and the head of the talus is pushed down and medially.

blocks.answer: Loss of tibialis posterior support flattens the medial longitudinal arch.

items: Knee: ACL (anterior tibial translation), PCL (posterior tibial translation), tibial collateral (valgus), fibular collateral (varus).
Medial meniscus: attached to the tibial collateral ligament and therefore more often torn.
Unhappy triad: ACL, tibial collateral ligament and medial meniscus.
Foot arches: medial longitudinal, lateral longitudinal, transverse.

blocks.title: Direction of the ligament names
blocks.text: Anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments are named by their tibial attachment, not their femoral attachment, so the ACL passes from anterior tibia to lateral femoral condyle. Mixing these up reverses the answer to which ligament is tested in a drawer test.

points: Knee stability relies on four ligaments (ACL, PCL, tibial collateral, fibular collateral) and two menisci; the medial meniscus is attached to the tibial collateral ligament and torn more often.
An ACL tear follows a non-contact pivot, causes a pop and rapid haemarthrosis, and is detected by anterior drawer and Lachman tests.

The foot has medial longitudinal, lateral longitudinal and transverse arches, maintained by bone shape, ligaments such as the spring ligament and plantar aponeurosis, and tendons such as tibialis posterior and fibularis longus.

questions.stem: Which movement of the tibia on the femur does the anterior cruciate ligament primarily prevent?

distractorRationale.b: The PCL prevents backward sliding of the tibia.
distractorRationale.c: Valgus angulation is resisted by the tibial collateral ligament.
distractorRationale.d: Varus angulation is resisted by the fibular collateral ligament.

questions.explanation: The ACL runs from the anterior tibia to the lateral femoral condyle and checks forward translation of the tibia. This is why the anterior drawer and Lachman tests reveal an ACL tear.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old footballer pivots on a planted foot, hears a pop and develops a swollen knee within an hour. Lachman test shows increased forward movement of the tibia. Which structure is torn?

distractorRationale.b: A PCL tear shows excess posterior movement.
distractorRationale.c: A fibular collateral tear shows varus laxity.
distractorRationale.d: A patellar ligament tear prevents knee extension.

questions.explanation: A pop with rapid haemarthrosis after a pivoting injury and a positive Lachman test are classic for ACL rupture. Bleeding from the torn ligament, which lies inside the capsule, causes the early swelling.

questions.stem: Why is the medial meniscus injured more often than the lateral meniscus?

options.text: It is firmly attached to the tibial collateral ligament and therefore less mobile
It is smaller and more mobile
It is attached to the fibular collateral ligament
It has no attachment to the tibia

questions.correctOptionText: It is firmly attached to the tibial collateral ligament and therefore less mobile

distractorRationale.b: The lateral meniscus is the smaller, more mobile one.
distractorRationale.c: The fibular collateral ligament is not attached to the lateral meniscus.
distractorRationale.d: Both menisci attach to the tibia.

questions.explanation: The medial meniscus is anchored to the tibial collateral ligament, so it cannot move away from forces and is more easily torn. The lateral meniscus is more mobile and escapes injury more often.

questions.stem: Which ligament runs from the lateral femoral epicondyle to the head of the fibula?

distractorRationale.b: The tibial collateral runs on the medial side to the tibia.
distractorRationale.c: The ACL is inside the joint.
distractorRationale.d: The PCL is inside the joint.

questions.explanation: The fibular collateral ligament joins the lateral epicondyle of the femur to the head of the fibula and resists varus force. Unlike the tibial collateral ligament it does not attach to the meniscus.

questions.stem: Which structures are injured in the classic unhappy triad of the knee?

options.text: Anterior cruciate ligament, tibial collateral ligament and medial meniscus
Posterior cruciate ligament, fibular collateral ligament and lateral meniscus
Patellar ligament, quadriceps tendon and medial meniscus
Anterior cruciate ligament, fibular collateral ligament and lateral meniscus

questions.correctOptionText: Anterior cruciate ligament, tibial collateral ligament and medial meniscus

distractorRationale.b: These structures are not the classic triad.
distractorRationale.d: This combination involves the lateral side; the classic triad is medial.

questions.explanation: A valgus force with rotation on a planted foot damages the tibial collateral ligament, which is attached to the medial meniscus, and the ACL. The triad is therefore ACL, medial collateral ligament and medial meniscus.

questions.stem: Which ligament supports the head of the talus and helps maintain the medial longitudinal arch?

distractorRationale.b: The long plantar ligament supports the lateral longitudinal arch.
distractorRationale.c: The anterior talofibular ligament is a lateral ankle ligament.
distractorRationale.d: The tibial collateral ligament is in the knee.

questions.explanation: The spring ligament spans the calcaneus and navicular beneath the head of the talus, supporting the medial longitudinal arch. Failure of this ligament, often together with tibialis posterior, allows the arch to collapse.

questions.stem: True or false: the posterior cruciate ligament prevents the tibia from sliding forward on the femur.

distractorRationale.a: The PCL prevents backward sliding of the tibia; the ACL prevents forward sliding.

questions.explanation: The posterior cruciate ligament prevents the tibia from sliding backwards on the femur. Forward translation is restrained by the anterior cruciate ligament.

questions.stem: Which tendon helps maintain the transverse arch of the foot by passing across the sole from lateral to medial?

distractorRationale.b: Tibialis anterior supports the medial arch but does not cross the sole.
distractorRationale.c: Extensor hallucis longus is on the dorsum.
distractorRationale.d: The Achilles tendon inserts on the calcaneus and does not support the arches in this manner.

questions.explanation: The fibularis longus tendon passes behind the lateral malleolus and across the sole to the medial cuneiform and first metatarsal, bracing the transverse arch. With tibialis anterior it forms a stirrup supporting the arches.

questions.stem: Describe the mechanism of injury of the anterior cruciate ligament, its attachments and the clinical tests used to detect a tear.
markingGuide: ACL runs from the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia to the medial surface of the lateral femoral condyle.
Prevents forward movement of the tibia on the femur.
Mechanism: non-contact pivot, sudden deceleration or hyperextension.
Features: pop, rapid haemarthrosis and giving way.
Tests: anterior drawer test (about 90 degrees of flexion) and Lachman test (about 20 to 30 degrees); positive when the tibia moves forward excessively.
questions.explanation: The ligament's attachments dictate its function and thus the direction of the tests. Bleeding from the torn ligament within the capsule explains the early swelling.

questions.stem: Describe the arches of the foot and the structures that maintain them.
markingGuide: Three arches: medial longitudinal, lateral longitudinal, transverse.
Medial: calcaneus, talus, navicular, cuneiforms and medial three metatarsals; high and springy.
Lateral: calcaneus, cuboid, lateral two metatarsals; low and rigid.
Supports: bone shape, plantar aponeurosis, spring ligament, long and short plantar ligaments.
Tendons: tibialis posterior, tibialis anterior, fibularis longus, flexor hallucis longus, and intrinsic muscles.
questions.explanation: The arches distribute weight and provide a spring during walking. Both passive ligaments and active tendons support them, so tendon failure may produce flat foot.
